title.value: Safety and efficacy of sargramostim (GM‐CSF) in the treatment of Alzheimer's disease
title.quote: Safety and efficacy of sargramostim (GM‐CSF) in the treatment of Alzheimer's disease

design.value: randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase II trial
design.quote: We carried out a randomized, double‐blind, placebo‐controlled phase II trial to test the safety and efficacy of sargramostim treatment in mild‐to‐moderate AD participants

phase.quote: We carried out a randomized, double‐blind, placebo‐controlled phase II trial to test the safety and efficacy of sargramostim treatment

n.quote: were randomized to receive either sargramostim (20 participants, standard Food and Drug Administration dosage 250 mcg/m 2 /day subcutaneous injection [SC], 5 days/week for 3 weeks) or placebo (20 participants, SC saline

n_description.value: randomized: 20 participants to sargramostim and 20 participants to placebo
n_description.quote: Participants who met eligibility criteria (Table ) were randomized to receive either sargramostim (20 participants, standard Food and Drug Administration dosage 250 mcg/m 2 /day subcutaneous injection [SC], 5 days/week for 3 weeks)

population.value: Participants with clinically diagnosed mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease and a screening MMSE score of 10 to 26 inclusive
population.quote: mild‐to‐moderate AD participants, defined by clinical diagnosis and a screening Mini‐Mental State Examination (MMSE) score of 10 to 26 inclusive

followup.value: 5 days/week for 3 weeks of treatment plus follow-up visits at 45 days (FU1) and 90 days (FU2) after end of treatment
followup.quote: Treatments (20 participants/group) occurred 5 days/week for 3 weeks plus two follow‐up (FU) visits (FU1 at 45 days and FU2 at 90 days) with neurological, neuropsychological, blood biomarker, and imaging assessments.

intervention.value: sargramostim (GM-CSF/leukine) 250 mcg/m2/day subcutaneous injection, 5 days/week for 3 weeks
intervention.quote: sargramostim (20 participants, standard Food and Drug Administration dosage 250 mcg/m 2 /day subcutaneous injection [SC], 5 days/week for 3 weeks)

comparator.value: placebo (subcutaneous saline), 5 days/week for 3 weeks, 20 participants
comparator.quote: or placebo (20 participants, SC saline, 5 days/week for 3 weeks)

biomarker_confirmation.value: Amyloid-PET imaging was an inclusion criterion for the second half of the study; all 16 participants so assessed were amyloid-positive
biomarker_confirmation.quote: For the second half of the study, amyloid‐PET imaging was used as an inclusion criterion. All 16 participants diagnosed as having mild‐to‐moderate AD at screening, who were then assessed by amyloid‐PET imaging, were found to be amyloid‐positive

outcomes.name: Safety (drug-related serious adverse events, including amyloid-related imaging abnormalities)
outcomes.prespecification_evidence:
Primary endpoint: safety and innate immune system activation

- Short‐term sargramostim treatment in mild‐to‐moderate AD participants increased innate immune cell and cytokine measures and was safe and well tolerated.
outcomes.effect_estimate: no drug-related serious adverse events and no amyloid-related imaging abnormalities
outcomes.quote: Data and Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB) assessments of study events found no drug‐related serious adverse events (SAEs), including no amyloid‐related imaging abnormalities

limitations: Although this trial was small and thus inherently underpowered, several secondary/exploratory outcomes were statistically significant.
The main weaknesses are the short treatment period, small sample size, especially in the amyloid‐PET substudy, and non‐memory cognitive measures, showing no direct treatment effects.
However, the powers of the tests are limited by the small number of participants.
the main conclusion of the study is that additional longer, larger trials of GM‐CSF/sargramostim in AD are warranted
The article indicates that a larger, longer trial of GM‐CSF/sargramostim in AD is warranted.
An extended treatment trial testing the long‐term safety and efficacy of GM‐CSF/sargramostim in AD is warranted.

risk_of_bias.judgement: Mean MMSE scores differed statistically significantly between the sargramostim and placebo groups at baseline, and the primary MMSE analysis used an unadjusted cell means model
risk_of_bias.quote: although the mean MMSE scores at screening were not significantly different between the sargramostim and placebo groups, they were at baseline (–3.65, 95% confidence interval [CI]: [–6.71, 0.59], P = .0207)

risk_of_bias.domain: interim result disclosure during an ongoing trial
risk_of_bias.judgement: The authors reported interim study results at symposia in 2018 while the trial was ongoing, and tested afterwards for resulting bias
risk_of_bias.quote: Because we reported interim study results at symposia in 2018, we tested for a potential subsequent bias and found no significant difference between the mean total MMSE scores of participants enrolled during the first and second halves of the trial.

risk_of_bias.judgement: The document states the trial was small and inherently underpowered, and that the amyloid-PET substudy tests had limited power
risk_of_bias.quote: Although this trial was small and thus inherently underpowered, several secondary/exploratory outcomes were statistically significant.

risk_of_bias.judgement: Two authors are inventors on U.S. patents and one became an employee of a company selling sargramostim
risk_of_bias.quote: Drs. Potter and Boyd are two of the inventors on several U.S. patents owned by the University of South Florida, but not licensed. As of Feb.1 2021, Dr. Boyd is an employee of Partner Therapeutics.

disagreements.question: Is inflammation solely detrimental in Alzheimer's disease?
disagreements.position: This document argues its GM-CSF findings call the consensus view into question, holding that stimulating rather than suppressing the innate immune system can be beneficial in AD
disagreements.attributed_to: the authors of this article (Potter, Woodcock, Boyd et al.)
disagreements.quote: These results called into question the consensus view that inflammation is solely detrimental in AD.

disagreements.question: Are general anti-inflammatory drugs or targeted immune modulators the better therapeutic strategy in AD?
disagreements.position: Given the failure of NSAID trials, this document argues targeted modulators of neuroinflammation may be a better therapeutic strategy than general anti-inflammatory drugs
disagreements.quote: suggests that targeted modulators of neuroinflammation may be a better therapeutic strategy than general anti‐inflammatory drugs
